newsitem.title: USA: PHLX units settle U.S. SEC administrative charges.
newsitem.headline: PHLX units settle U.S. SEC administrative charges.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday said two subsidiaries of the Philadelphia Stock Exchange agreed to settle the agency's allegations that they failed to comply with some of their own rules.

The SEC brought its case against the Stock Clearing Corp of Philadelphia and Philadelphia Depository Trust Co, which process and guarantee trades made on the Philadelphia exchange. As part of the settlement, the clearing unit agreed to limit its services, while the depository arm agreed to exit the business.

In its order, the SEC noted that the Philadelphia clearing and depository subsidiaries are "self-regulatory organizations (SROs)," a designation obligating them to operate by and enforce their own rules, as approved by the agency, and federal securities laws.
"If there is any message from this case it's that the commission expects SROs to take their rules and their SRO obligations seriously," an official in the SEC's Philadelphia office said.

The SEC alleged among other things that the two units did not follow their own rules on safeguarding participants' funds. It also alleged that the clearing subsidiary did not follow its rule requiring it to use the current market price when "marking-to-the market" participants' valued positions.
"What we've got here are a myriad of instances ... where time and time and time again there were problems," an SEC official added.
The boards of the Philadelphia exchange units were ordered to make a minimum of a $5-million commitment of capital over a three-year period to fund certain undertakings.

Of that, the SEC directed the units to put $3 million toward establish a reserve fund to cover expected operating expenses. The agency wants the subsidiaries to revamp compliance and to set up and maintain a back-up power supply Philadelphia Stock Exchange President Nicholas Giordano stressed that the SEC's case was an administrative one and he noted that there were no fines levied.
"There was never an issue of fraud," he said. "We're pleased to get this thing behind us."

The SEC also settled a separate "cease-and-desist" proceeding against Timothy Guiheen, former president of the two Philadelphia exchange subsidiaries. The exchange subsidiaries and Guiheen settled the agency's charges without admitting or denying the findings.
